title: Automate your A/B test readouts
description: A system that turns your A/B test results into a plain-language readout naming the outcome, the uncertainty behind it, and one recommended next step.

pull.title: Pull
pull.content: Downloading the latest changes from GitHub to your computer so your local copy is up to date. Claude pulls before starting work to make sure it's building on the newest version, not an old one.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

slack.title: Slack
slack.content: The team messaging app most companies run on. In Level 2, students connect Slack to their AI tools to trigger workflows from messages, post AI-generated updates to channels, or summarize threads automatically.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

notion.title: Notion
notion.content: An all-in-one workspace for docs, wikis, databases, and project tracking. Used heavily across the AI Builder program as a destination for AI-generated content and as a connected app in Level 2 automations.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

read-only.title: Read-only
read-only.content: The first rung of the trust gradient: the agent can see your inbox, calendar, or docs but can't change anything. The default starting state for every new tool connection. Tiny blast radius, fast to ship, and confirms the read side works before you graduate the write side.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: Checking a test's results before it reaches its planned sample size, "peeking," can inflate a nominal 5% significance threshold to as high as 26.1%, per [Evan Miller's "How Not to Run an A/B Test."](https://www.evanmiller.org/how-not-to-run-an-ab-test.html) A lot of declared wins never get checked against that math. This system reads your test-versus-control data and returns a readout of the outcome, its uncertainty, and one recommended next step instead of a single "we won" headline.

OpenAI's own product playbook frames the job narrowly on purpose. It has the AI identify significance and which metrics moved, then recommend next steps, never declare a winner outright. That discipline matters most when a launch decision rides on the readout.

Run it as a paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) each time a test hits its stopping point, a saved skill, or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) [pulling](#tooltip-pull) straight from your experimentation tool. Every version stays [read-only](#tooltip-read-only) against your test data.

Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming your results source, what the readout always covers, how to handle a test that isn't yet significant, and who reads it.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that turns my A/B test results into a readable readout. Ask me questions, one at a time, about what testing tool my results come from, what the readout should always cover, how to handle a test that isn't yet significant, and who reads these. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the interview forces the stopping rule and the required fields into writing before a single result gets read.

items: Which platform your results come from, and whether that needs a connector or a manual export.
Whether your team already pre-registers a stopping rule, or needs one built before this runs.
What the readout must always include, confidence interval and segment differences, versus what's optional.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather any access it calls for. Common [connectors](#tooltip-tool-connectors) are an experimentation tool (Statsig, Amplitude), a sheet if results are pulled manually, and a docs tool to deliver the readout ([Notion](#tooltip-notion), [Slack](#tooltip-slack)). The paste-in version needs none.

**Create.** Start building the system your scope document describes, and test it on a real results export. The prompt below is an example of the core task. Your scope document will give you a version shaped to your setup.

children.prompt:
Goal: Turn raw test results into a plain-language readout with a clear recommendation.

Context: [Paste your results export: treatment vs. control, sample sizes, and the metrics tracked.] [Your pre-registered primary metric and any guardrail metrics.] [Your planned sample size or stopping date.]

Rules:
- State whether the pre-set sample size was reached before this readout was run.
- Report the primary metric's result with its confidence interval, not a single point estimate.
- Note any segment differences worth flagging, and label them as a hypothesis, not a conclusion.
- Never call a result a "winner" if the test was stopped early.
- End with one clear recommendation: ship, hold, or extend the test.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: requiring the confidence interval and the stopping-rule check up front blocks the shortcut straight to a headline.

children.text: **Review.** Check against your scope. Sample size confirmed, interval stated, segments labeled as hypotheses, one recommendation given?
**Feedback.** Correct the rule that let the gap through, so it stays fixed for the next test.

items: Flag any test checked before its planned end date.
Log every test's outcome against the recommendation it got.
Require the stopping rule to be locked before a test even launches.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric) instead of a feel check. Have your AI chat draft the rubric and a run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each test readout, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for test name, sample size reached, primary metric result, recommendation given, and outcome after launch. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the outcome column is what turns the log into a track record instead of a pile of past readouts.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Each entry takes a minute. Note the date, which rubric checks passed or failed, and what you changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the system passes the rubric a few tests straight, package the prompt and your corrected rules into a reusable AI skill. A check that fails again and again is a candidate for a skill of its own. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s built-in skill-creator skill will interview you and write the skill for you, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).
One durable failure mode. It can't know if a test was peeked at early, so that discipline has to be enforced upstream. Treat any segment breakdown it surfaces as a hypothesis worth testing further.

items: [Evan Miller, How Not to Run an A/B Test](https://www.evanmiller.org/how-not-to-run-an-ab-test.html) — The peeking-inflates-significance stat.
[OpenAI Academy, ChatGPT for product](https://academy.openai.com/public/clubs/work-users-ynjqu/resources/use-cases-product) — The significance-and-next-steps framing.
